newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: African Bank meet ends early, reforms applauded.
newsitem.headline: African Bank meet ends early, reforms applauded.

text.p: The annual meeting of the African Development Bank ended a day earlier than planned on Thursday after a more harmonious assembly than in recent years.
Over the two days, governors from both African and Western countries lined up to congratulate AfDB President Omar Kabbaj on his success in reforming the Bank over the past two years.

Canada's representative, Carolyn McAskie, welcomed the "notable progress" made and announced that the Western countries had agreed as a result to release a second tranche of funds for the Bank's soft loan arm, the African Development Fund.

That $3.2 billion replenishment was delayed for two years until May 1996 because Western shareholders were not happy with management practices. The Fund was effectively frozen, and the 39 African countries that borrow from it were hit hard.
These hard-up countries are no longer allowed to borrow from the Bank itself since they are not deemed creditworthy.

Some African countries believe the restrictions are too tight -- Sudan's representative complained of "hard and punitive measures" and said the AfDB was losing its "African authenticity" -- but Bank officials said they were working.

Although some speakers worried about the level of arrears owed the Bank and the effect this might have on the Bank's standing in financial markets, Treasurer Thierry de Longuemar said they had not fully appreciated the progress made.

"The mechanisms put in place to reduce the arrears have already shown their effectiveness -- in 1996 by cutting the rhythm at which they progressed, and above all in 1997 when the volume of arrears should be reduced substantially," he said.
So far this year Congo, Cameroon, Niger and Madagascar had paid off their arrears. Another country was set to do the same, he said, but he would not name it until the deal was complete.
The bulk of the arrears are owed by countries going through political or social strife.

By far the biggest sum is owed by the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, with 329 million units of account, or around $474 million, in arrears at the end of 1996, when the total owed by 11 countries was 576 million units of account.
Congo, Madagascar, Angola, Liberia and, to a lesser extent, Somalia, were also significantly in arrears at that time.
The other main topic of discussion at the meeting was the thorny question of the capital increase Kabbaj is seeking.
Some Western shareholders wondered whether it was necessary, given the Bank's restricted lending in recent years, but most had come round to the idea by the close.
However, Western shareholders will have to cough up the money and want greater voting powers as a result.
Currently the non-regionals have one third of the shares and African states two-thirds.

U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told the meeting the U.S. wanted Western shareholders to have 45 percent of the vote plus "Executive Board voting rules that will ensure us a more effective voice in the organisation".
Nigeria, currently the Bank's biggest shareholder with 10 percent, sees no reason to change the status quo.
Kabbaj said he hoped a compromise would be found in time to put the matter before the 1998 annual meeting in Botswana.
"No one wants this sort of thing hanging over the group," said one European representative. "I'm confident that something will be agreed in 1998."
